title: Dogen on Enlightenment
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Here is a summary of the talk's main teaching in plain language: Nomon Tim Burnett emphasizes that enlightenment and practice are not separate entities, but rather interconnected aspects of the Buddhist path. Through zazen (seated meditation), we can directly experience our true nature, which is beyond words and concepts, and drop away all dualistic thinking and distinctions between subject and object. The goal of zazen is not to achieve a specific state or experience, but rather to reveal our true nature, allowing us to live more authentically and peacefully in the present moment.

Can you hear me?
Can you hear me okay?
Yeah?
Okay.
Good.
Well, thank you again for deciding to join us.

It's a really interesting experiment, having our first Red Cedar Zen seven-day Rohatsu sesshin, traditional days, at least traditional days once the Japanese switched from the lunar calendar to the solar calendar.
December 1 through 8.

Originally, the Japanese decided somehow, I don't know how, that the Buddha's enlightenment was on the morning of the eighth day of the twelfth moon, but that would be different days on the Gregorian calendar, but then they decided to modernize.
So it's on December 8, for sure, just like Jesus was born on December 25, for sure.
So interesting that we're doing this online.
So thanks for trying that.

Also, I wanted to mention, in case you didn't know yet, Daikon here, our wonderful Tenkin, is being kind enough to offer us 10 minutes of Han music before each time we come back, and 10 minutes before the official zazen start time, so like 9:50 as opposed to 10, or 6:50 as opposed to 7.
So why don't we treat this like a Zen sesshin and not like a Zoom meeting and show up a little before the time so we can enjoy sitting together and listening to the music of the Han.
Such a blessing.
So what to talk about during our talks?
I'll be giving several talks.
Chris, Shudo Chris, will give several talks.
Plenty [unclear: "is for"] Kanchi and Allison to give some talks.
We're just waiting to see how her health is.
So Rohatsu, the word actually means something like 8-12, eighth day, twelfth month.
Since it's all about the Buddha's awakening, we were talking about it and we thought, well, we should talk about awakening, we should talk about enlightenment.
And that's hard to talk about, beyond words and all that.
So I was thinking about how Dogen really taught that it's a mistake to think about enlightenment or awakening as somehow separate from everything else.
He came up with this idea, or he experienced and really felt, was really clear in his heart, this understanding, not just an idea.

Enlightenment is not some special experience that you have later because of the accumulated power of your practice, which is a little bit like what the heroic story of the Buddha's awakening sounds like.
Practice hard all those years, tried these practices with these teachers and mastered them because he was such a prodigy, right, but that didn't really get him all the way there.
Tried the grueling ascetic practices, mastered those too, and there are those wonderful and frightening statues of the Buddha with just his ribcage showing.
No body left practically, but that didn't get him there.
And then finally landing on the just right practice, the middle way practice that got him there, which is an instructive story and a good story.
But I think Dogen didn't really buy that story because of the way it separates the effort from the enlightenment.
He really felt like practice and enlightenment were not two separate things, but not exactly one thing either.
So there's this wonderful idea in Buddhist dialectics of not two.
Practice and enlightenment are not two.
They're not two different things, but it seems a little too simple to say they're one thing because we do need to practice.
So why would that be true if practice and enlightenment were one thing?

So as you know, Dogen came up with this phrase, practice enlightenment, that we are Buddha nature, and it made me think of the wonderful little koan he quotes at the end of Genjokoan, which we'll chant in the morning a few days from now.
It talks about this idea of practice enlightenment and yet we still need to practice.
Practice and enlightenment, not two, not one.
So remember the story.
*Zen master Baochu of Mt.
Mayu was fanning himself with a fan.
A monk approached and said, Master, the nature of wind is permanent.
There's no place it doesn't reach.
Why do you need to fan yourself?
Master replies, although you understand that the nature of wind is permanent, you do not understand the meaning of its reaching everywhere.
What's the meaning of its reaching everywhere, asked the monk.
The master just kept fanning himself.
The monk bowed deeply.*
The monk thinks stories are very persistent, you know.
And then Dogen comments on the story.
He says:
*The actualization of the Buddha Dharma, the vital path of its correct transmission, is like this.*
It's like this story.
If you say you don't need to fan yourself because the nature of wind is permanent, because wind is everywhere, why would you need to fan yourself?
Then you don't get it, right?
You understand neither permanence nor the nature of wind.
So here, of course, wind represents awakening, represents enlightenment.
And even though the wind is everywhere in all things, so enlightenment is everywhere in all things.
And permanent here is an odd choice, right, because we know everything's impermanent.
But usually what we're talking about when we say everything's impermanent is the vast realm of the conditioned, where we hang out and do our thinking and talking, the realm of the conditioned.
So permanent in the story points to the unconditioned, beyond conditioning.
And so the monk's right.
Enlightenment, the wind, the unconditioned, the permanent is everywhere.
So why do we need to practice?
Why do we need to fan ourselves?
And of course Dogen says, exactly, exactly, that's why you need to practice.
So no simple answer there, right?
We have to learn this for ourselves.
Keep practicing, keep fanning ourselves.
And of course our suffering will remind us, even if our big heads try to tuck ourselves into some philosophical position, right?

You can sit around saying to yourself, oh, we're already enlightened, but if you're miserable and dissatisfied with this beautiful life you've been given, you realize, oh, maybe so, but I'd better practice.
And I looked up the term Dogen coined, practice enlightenment.
I've been meaning to do this for ages.
In Japanese it's something like shuso itto, four characters.
And the four characters mean study, verify, one suchness.
Study, verify, one suchness.
So it's a very active phrase, study and verify, practice.
And one is in there, there's a connection here, there's a oneness, even if it's not just oneness, to this suchness, to things just as they are, right?
To the wind, to enlightenment.
And the other thing that's interesting is the first character, study, also another synonym there is discipline.
So this is a very vigorous, disciplined practice, you probably noticed that.
So anyway, I was thinking about all this, back to the dharma talk topic, and I was thinking, well, that's good, we can talk about zazen, because there's some tangibility to zazen.
It's something that we are trying to do with our bodies and our minds and our hearts.
So who knows what enlightenment is, but we can talk about zazen.

So I thought, well, maybe we go over one of Dogen's wonderful texts about zazen, like Fukanzazengi that we'll chant tomorrow morning, or maybe one of his lesser known texts, like there's two different texts by Dogen called Zazengi, and we should study those sometimes.

But then I thought further, and I was inspired because I got to work with some of our priests the other day, and we were reviewing what the National Organization of Soto Zen Priests thinks that the priests should all understand and be able to do and study and be able to live.
There's a list of standards.
Do you know there's a National Organization of Soto Zen Priests?
It's not a large organization, there's not that many of us.
Anyway, on their list was to be sure to not just study Dogen, although there's a lot about Dogen on their list, but to not neglect the other famous Japanese Zen ancestor, founder, named Keizan.
And we don't think much about Keizan because we're always studying Dogen.

And Keizan also wrote an important text on zazen called Zazengyojinki, in the title that means something like, using zazen to remember the heart and mind, or practicing zazen to remember the heart and mind.
So I thought, well, maybe we should study that.
So that's where I landed.
So Keizan is far from forgotten in Japanese Soto Zen.
He's very important because he's seen as the founder of the larger of the two headquarters temples of the Soto Zen school, Soto Shu.
He's considered the founder of Sojiji in Yokohama on the edge of Kyoto, which is a great big place.
It's like a college campus.
The Buddha Hall, I think, is in some way the largest Zen hall in the universe.
It's made out of concrete, built in the 50s, I think.
It has over a thousand tatami mats inside.
It's a great big place.
And of course, to say that Keizan is the founder is the usual religious enthusiasm.
He really founded a whole different temple called Yokoji on the other side of Japan, but through various religious historical enthusiasm, he's the founder of that.
And Japanese Zen, the way it's organized, is a little bit like a pyramid scheme, where each temple has temples beneath it, and they have temples beneath them, and they have temples beneath them.
And guess what you do?
You make a donation to the temple above you.

So there's these two at the top, Eiheiji, that we've all heard about probably, because that's what Dogen really did found on the Sea of Japan side of things, and Sojiji here by Tokyo on the other side of the country, other side of Honshu.
So any Japanese Zen person in Japan would right away recognize Keizan, but we don't think that much about Keizan.
So I thought we should give Keizan his due.
Probably don't think about it much because we're so Western, and we think about texts and philosophy and the ideas of enlightenment.
And Dogen was a prolific and important writer, as you know.
Keizan, who was just two generations later, depending on how you count, he was born a little bit after Dogen passed away.
He wrote plenty too, but I think philosophers and Buddhist studies scholars are less impressed.
He ain't Dogen.

His most important work is a series of stories on the chain of succession from Buddha through all the Indian ancestors to Bodhidharma and through all the Chinese ancestors, and all the way up to Dogen's first disciple named Eijo, and Eijo is Keizan's teacher's teacher.
So it's a wonderful enthusiastic book about stories and koans, basically about each ancestor, called Denko Roku.
And it represents also the wonderful mythology of Zen, about ancestors that we got from the Chinese.
And there's ancestral charts with these little lines going very tidily down to the next ancestor, the next ancestor.
Sometimes there are branches, if a teacher had a lot of disciples, little branch like a family tree, like family.
And although it's actually true that each of us in our biological family could only have one mother and father, it's not so true in real historical fact about Zen, but that's okay.
It's a wonderful, enthusiastic idea.
So that's Keizan's famous work.
They also wrote this important text about zazen, so I thought we'd look at that.
But a little more about Keizan himself, because he's a pretty cool guy actually, so it's good to bring him forward, especially these days.

Because Keizan, in this very patriarchal world of Japanese and Chinese Zen and Buddhism in general, sorry to say, being a male, white teacher talking to you now, what you already know, pretty male dominated throughout the centuries.
Now I think in American Zen, we have more or less the same number of male and female teachers.
Not so good on other kinds of diversity, we're trying.
So what's cool about Keizan in this dimension, at least, is he was as close as you could get in medieval Japan to being a feminist.
He was raised by his grandmother.
And it turns out his eventual closeness to Dogen's lineage and membership in Dogen's lineage was really preordained.
Because his grandmother was in society in Kyoto.
And she was one of Dogen's supporters when the young Dogen returned from China.
And as an adult, Keizan was also very close to his mother, who was a Buddhist nun.
Not ordained in the Soto Zen lineage, but a Buddhist nun.
Which is maybe why she didn't raise him.
I haven't found that out yet.
Why was he raised by his grandmother if he was close to his mother?
His mother was also like his Dharma advisor.
And as he got famous, his mother would show up periodically and talk him down, help him stay humble, which he always appreciated.
And he also helped his mother become appointed as an abbess of a small monastery, a place called Jojuji.

And the other thing that's cool about Keizan as a feminist, or, you know, they didn't have that term, but apparently he really appreciated women, is the first person he gave Dharma transmission to was his female student, Ekyuu.
And that also was the first Dharma transmission given to any woman in Soto Zen, ever, in Japan.
Apparently he also wanted a woman to be his Dharma heir, for this lineage chart that they were gradually building, generation after generation.
But I don't know if it was by fault of his own, but it didn't work out that way.
On your lineage chart, if you've received Chūkai, or priest ordination, you'll find a male name after Keizan Jōken, Daio Shō.
The other thing that's really cool about Keizan, and maybe it goes with this emphasis on the feminine in his life and practice, was that he really listened to dreams.
I'll look up the story, I couldn't remember it, for a future talk this week, hopefully.
He made several important life decisions based on what he remembered from experiences he had in his dream life.
That's a deep idea in practice.
In our Western materialism, we don't think about practicing in our dreams as much, but it's a deep idea in all practice traditions, I think.
You can practice with and within your dreams.
He even had notable dreams where his grandmother showed up after she passed away, directing him, and he would listen, follow the guidance of his dream grandmother.
Isn't that great?
But the real reason Keizan's important, why a Japanese Sōtō Zen person would of course be very familiar with his life and who he was, is that Keizan was an efficient organizer.

I don't know if the historians would agree perfectly, but probably if Keizan hadn't showed up, we would never be doing this, and we would never have heard of Dogen, because Dogen was a kind of [unclear: "class"].
Eiheiji, when Dogen died, was just two buildings, a small place, I don't know how many monks, 40, 50, maybe at the most.
Dogen being a purist and a serious, serious guy, he didn't run around popularizing anything.
He just did his practice and gave his talks and wrote them down, or his student Ejo wrote them down.
But Keizan knew how to organize.
He founded several temples, and his students went on to found several temples.
So the proliferation of Sōtō Zen was partly more through him than through Dogen.
Keizan also intelligently realized that they should dedicate merit of practice not just to bodhisattvas and buddhas, but to secular officials too, especially the local secular officials.
So he was a little bit crafty too, so you can get some funding.
We think of Buddhism as so pure, and we had a lot of resistance at Red Cedar Zen back in the day when we started having members and getting involved in money and stuff.
But Keizan realized, yeah, you've got to fund this somehow.
So Buddhism over the centuries has always been a little bit elitist in that way.
But at the same time, here's Keizan's real genius.
He was effective in tapping into the regional elite and actually staying away from the national imperial elite, because that would have blown the thing away.
He also was able to access the hearts of the farmers, the local people.
I'm pretty sure he was one of the innovators involved in doing jukai ceremonies, receiving the precepts and the rakusu, for non-monks, for lay people.
That was a Japanese innovation that he was involved in.
I need to triple check my facts there, but I'm pretty sure he was one of the monks that helped start that.
A lot of the farmers were illiterate, as poor farmers have been throughout history.
So receiving their lineage paper also had a real power, the written word with their Dharma name and maybe their secular name on it.
That helped cement Sōtō Zen as the Zen of the masses.
Even so, the other kind of Buddhism that was emerging about the same time, Pure Land Buddhism, was way more popular.
So don't let this get to our heads.
Zen has been a little fringy from the beginning.
We'd want to do all this Zazen anyway.
So let's open our hearts a little to Master Keizan: sincere, promoter of women, politically astute, but really caring about ordinary people, all at the same time.
Amazing.
So here's the opening paragraph of his text, Zazen Yojinki, using or practicing Zazen to remember the heart mind.
Okay.
I have all this electronically, so I'll try to send out the whole text at the end of retreat when you might want to look at it later.
Keizan wrote:
*Zazen allows people to directly enlighten the primordial mind and to abide peacefully in their original state.
This is known as realizing one's original face or manifesting the true nature of the primordial mind.
Zazen is the dropping off of body and mind and remaining detached, whether seated or lying down.
It's not concerned with good or evil.
It transcends the distinctions of worldly and sacred delusion and enlightenment, sentient beings and Buddhas.*
Let me reread that sentence.
*It transcends the distinctions of worldly and sacred delusion and enlightenment, sentient beings and Buddhas.

So Zazen as peace, right?
Letting go beyond good and evil, transcending delusion and enlightenment.
I'm really interested.
There's a four-up grid implied here, I think, where he says "worldly and sacred delusion and enlightenment."
Maybe there's just a missing comma, but I like that as a four-up thing, worldly and sacred delusion and enlightenment.
So they're suggesting maybe that there's worldly delusion and sacred delusion.
That's really worth contemplating.
It's really cool, I think.
We all know what worldly delusion is.
What might sacred delusion be?
Sacred delusion.
Norman's been are writing a lot lately about the pivotal importance of imagination.

Maybe that's sacred delusion.
It's not real, right?
So we're making this up.
We're imagining this.
But delusion has a negative connotation all by itself, and maybe it shouldn't.
Delusion itself sounds like worldly delusion: confused, wrong-headed ideas, being mixed up, greedy, self-focused, angry, missing the point.
But maybe delusion is not just negative like that.
Maybe there's sacred delusion, blissful vision.
And maybe that's really important.
Really important.
And also, there are these other two dimensions of this little four-by-four grid that I'm imputing in Dogen's work, or Keizan's work, sorry: worldly and sacred delusion and enlightenment.
So how about worldly and sacred enlightenment?
Worldly enlightenment, sacred enlightenment, also interesting.
Because Zen is so concerned with embracing the ordinary as sacred too, right?
The worldly enlightenment of just being here on this planet, in this life as it is.
So perhaps we're leaving Zazen behind a little bit here, because Zazen transcends even these ideas, right?
Beyond ideas.
It's wonderful to have more subtle and beautiful ideas about life than just being caught in our day-to-day suffering.
That's important.
That's uplifting, right?
We study.
We have a bigger vision.
Zazen says, go even further.
Go beyond all ideas, beyond sacred, beyond worldly, beyond enlightenment, beyond delusion.
And then Keizan repeats a Dogen phrase, dropping off body and mind.
This phrase, which is shinjin datsuraku in Japanese, is kind of a big deal.
It looks like Dogen took a phrase he heard in China with his teacher and gave it some twists, as he always did.
I looked this up and I ran into this Buddhist studies article, like 10 pages long, about this phrase, dropping off body and mind, shinjin datsuraku.
Some theories are that maybe Dogen actually just misunderstood and made up his own meaning.
I don't know.
I don't think we have to worry too much.
But it's an important idea, an important feeling, this idea of dropping off body and mind as Zazen.
So maybe we could just think about it as fully letting go while being fully present, dropping off body and mind.
Let's play with that in Zazen and in between Zazen, which is also still Zazen.
What would letting go and being fully present be?
Because letting go could sound a little bit like drifting off somewhere or going somewhere else, but feeling fully present could be a little bit like we're holding on to something.

Or maybe sometimes in Zazen, a simpler phrase or words that point to something emerge.
Lately, what's been coming up for me during Zazen, from time to time, not all the time, on the in-breath, is "opening."
Right, opening.
On the out-breath, "healing."
Opening, healing.
You can practice that if you like.
Opening, healing, fully present, letting go.
All kinds of words could be helpful.
But also remember that this is not a mind trip.
Zazen is body-mind practice.
So maybe Rohatsu and looking at Keizan's teaching on Zazen can encourage us to take a fresh look at posture.
How is the body being practiced through?
Posture sounds a little bit like this mechanical thing, like arrange it right, set it up right.
But the body is not mechanical, right?
The body is alive, living and changing all the time.
So I've been looking a little bit at posture, and I've been concerned and curious about the way I tend to hunch forward.
Maybe most of us hunch forward a little bit.
So I've been working with a yoga therapist.
It's been interesting, just getting started.
Her first suggestion, I recommend, let's see if I can, it's hard to show on camera, is this: the hunch-forward posture has the arms kind of rolled in.
So here's what she suggested.
Try this right now.
Keep your elbows at your sides and bring your arms out.
Just rotate your arms out to the side and let your shoulders relax, breathe, soften.
Even bring your arms back a little further and rotate the hands a little bit, like you're holding a platter and there's a danger that the stuff on the platter is going to fall off behind you.
You feel that?
Give it a little time, breathe into it.
If there's tension and discomfort, be gentle.
Maybe you don't go all the way back.
I can't quite go all the way back myself.
Feel how that encourages the upper arms to rotate out, lets the shoulders drop and the scapula come together.
The sternum lifts a little bit, right?
Maybe the upper spine just gently rises up to support the lifted sternum.
If you stay with it, maybe you start to notice a little more space for the neck and head.
Then the interesting thing is to see if you can establish something of that feeling and keep the upper arms rotated out as you drop your hands back to your lap and [unclear: "make your road trip"].
You'll lose it sooner or later.
If you're conditioned like my body, from all this hunching forward, looking at the screen or whatever, I think it started in childhood, probably before computers were invented.
So there's an openness to the Zazen posture.
Then the whole thing also needs to be planted, right?
You need a basis, you need a support.
So how is the pelvis on the cushion or the chair?
Are you planted in a way that maybe the pelvis is tilted forward slightly?
That's helpful.
And maybe, just checking out the whole upper body, you could rock it a little bit forward and back.
Is it balanced?
Sometimes our internal imagining of where up and down is, just called proprioception in psychology, physiology, is a little off.
So let gravity tell you more than your head.
Because of this hunching-forward thing, I'm so normalized to that that what feels straight up and down is actually leaning forward a little bit.
So maybe leaning back a little bit, to my internal sense, is actually vertical.
Again, [unclear: "in case in both"], as we'll soon see, probably next talk, they care about this, they bring it up.
So it's dropping off body and mind, and we do it through the body, the upright, open body.
This idea we somehow got somewhere that the body and mind are separate systems is, of course, ridiculous.

If you just think about it for a minute, if the mind is something to do with the brain, which seems like it must, something like the brain fully explains the mind, but without the brain, no mind, right?
And the brain is part of this massive nervous system, which of course runs through the whole body, right?
There's nervous system stuff everywhere.
Do you know there's 100 million neurons in your gut?
So the mind is everywhere in the body and the body is the mind.
So we're practicing zazen with the body-mind.
That's what drops away.
That's what can be fully present and fully letting go.
If that feels a little awkward, be gentle with yourself.

Don't get too uptight, because there's a very easy fallacy here, with all this paying more attention to the posture: you do another level of separation of the mind from the posture, and the mind is like the boss saying, "Get it together, Tim, sit properly, don't be a slouch," right?
And then there's a lot of tension, and a lot of getting upset at yourself.
So: fully present and letting go, and letting go.
So that's the first paragraph.
Here it is again, at least my riff on it.
*Zazen allows people, us, to directly enlighten the primordial mind and abide peacefully in the original state.
This is known as realizing one's original face or manifesting the true nature of the primordial mind.
Zazen is the dropping off of body and mind and remaining detached, whether seated or lying down.
It is not concerned with good or evil and transcends the distinctions of worldly and sacred, delusion and enlightenment, sentient beings and Buddhas.
It relinquishes the ten thousand things, renounces all conditions, casts aside everything, does not rely on the six senses.*
So one could say, well, let's go on to the second paragraph, so we have a sense of momentum.
Keizan goes on to say:
*What is this that is nameless and cannot be identified with either body or mind?
If you try to conceive of it, it is beyond thought.
If you try to express it, words are exhausted.
It appears both foolish and saintly.
It is as high as the mountain and as deep as the ocean, yet discloses neither height nor depth.
It is illuminatively unbound, [unclear: "cut by"] conditions, displaying a radiance that cannot be discerned by the naked eye.
It penetrates beyond thought and has clarity above the entanglements of speech.
It transcends both heaven and earth, and is realized only by the entire person.*
Not a whole lot to say.
I'll just read it again, because this is the counterpart to the first paragraph, right?
He said a bunch of words and now he's going to say, well, actually, it's beyond words.
*What is this that is nameless and cannot be identified with body or mind?
If you try to conceive of it, it's beyond thought.
If you try to express it, words are exhausted.
It appears both foolish and saintly.
It is as high as the mountains and as deep as the ocean, yet it discloses neither height nor depth.
It is unbound by conditions, displaying a radiance that cannot be discerned by the naked eye.
It penetrates beyond thought and has clarity above the entanglements of speech.
It transcends both heaven and earth and is realized only by the entire person.*
Beyond the body and mind.
Beyond.
Don't be limited by any idea.
Of course, he's going to go on and give us lots more ideas.
So this is typical Zen stuff.
But it's true, right?
It's really true.
Ideas are beyond ideas, beyond ideas.
So let's just do the third paragraph, and that'll be plenty for today, I think.
Here's the third paragraph, which is pretty interesting.
*It is like an immeasurably perfected person who has experienced the great death, of Parinirvana, and has an unobstructed vision and unhindered action.
What dust defiles it?
What obstacle can block it?
Clear water originally has neither front nor back.
Empty space is not bound by inside or outside.
Zazen has a pristine clarity that is self-illuminating prior to distinctions of form and emptiness, subject and object.
It's eternal but can never be named.
The third patriarch, Senkan, referred to it as mind, and Nagarjuna referred to it as body.
It manifests the form of Buddha nature and actualizes the body of all Buddhas.

This mind is nothing other than Buddha.

One more time.
There's a lot there, isn't there?
Sorry.
This is also a good Zen Dharma experience: to play with original texts and be baffled by them.
So you just breathe with it, you don't worry too much.
*Zazen is like an immeasurably perfected person who has experienced the great death of Parinirvana and has unobstructed vision and unhindered action.
What dust can defile it?
What obstacles can block it?
Clear water originally has neither front nor back.
Empty space is not bound by inside or outside.
Zazen has a pristine clarity that's self-illuminating.
It is eternal, can never be named.
The third patriarch, Senkan, referred to it as mind.
Nagarjuna referred to it as body.
It manifests the form of Buddha nature and actualizes the body of all Buddhas.

Who is this person?
Who is it that sits, right?
What is it that sits?

Who is this I, in this ultimate powerful way that zazen is revealing to us?
Well, first he says it's like somebody who's let go so completely, they've died.
Let go into nirvana and passed on, not even holding onto the body.
It's so peaceful that dust can't settle on you.
You're clear like water, you're open like space, and it's not something you do.
So there's a powerful phrase in here: "Zazen has a pristine clarity that is self-illuminating."
Self-illuminating.
And Dogen talked about similar stuff.
You've heard about his self-fulfilling samadhi, jijuyu zanmai.
So somehow zazen does zazen, right?
Zazen takes care of itself.

So now we've got to bring up some ancestors.
